planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting 2-3 inches deep with growing tip up; this is one of the most widely distributed trilliums in the world, ranging from the Himalaya across China to Korea and Japan.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall in moist, humus-rich, well-drained, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade, setting the rhizome 2 to 3 inches deep with the growing tip pointed upward. Trillium tschonoskii is a smaller-statured, waxy-white-flowered species with an unusually broad natural range stretching from montane forests of the Himalaya eastward across central China to Korea and Japan, making it one of the most geographically adaptable trilliums in cultivation; the petals typically age to soft pink or purple as the bloom matures. Like other trilliums it takes five to seven years to flower from seed, so purchase only nursery-propagated divisions rather than wild-collected plants. Its compact habit suits it well to smaller shaded borders and rock garden woodland pockets where larger trillium species would crowd the space.

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall, setting 1-2 inches deep in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained woodland soil in partial shade; this naturally dwarf form stays only a few inches tall and suits raised beds, troughs, and rock garden woodland pockets better than open borders.

directions: Plant rhizome divisions in fall, 1-2 inches deep, in gritty, humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade with brighter light than the species typically tolerates, which helps keep the naturally compact habit tight and floriferous. First found on Vancouver Island by collector W. B. Hibberson, this miniature form of the western trillium reaches only a few inches in height yet produces a flower nearly as large as the full-sized species, an exaggerated proportion that makes it a favorite among alpine and rock garden collectors. It is slow-growing and best increased by careful rhizome division rather than seed, since seedlings frequently revert toward normal-sized western trillium. Excellent in a raised trough or scree bed where its scale won't be lost among larger woodland companions.

planting.note: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; give this Japanese species the same cool, consistently moist conditions preferred by other temperate Arisaema.

directions: Plant tubers 3-4 inches deep in early spring in moist, humus-rich, acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade. Arisaema urashima takes its name from the Japanese folk hero Urashima Taro, whose fishing line the spadix's remarkable appendage is said to resemble: from the tip of the green-and-white striped spathe trails an extraordinarily long, thread-like filament that can dangle a foot or more below the flower, unlike anything else in the jack-in-the-pulpit genus. The trifoliate leaves emerge alongside the flower and remain attractive through summer before the plant goes dormant. As with other Arisaema, the tuber slowly produces offsets to form a colony over years, and all plant parts contain calcium oxalate crystals that make them irritating if handled or eaten raw. A striking conversation-piece species for the serious woodland or collector's shade garden.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial shade; katakuri goes fully summer-dormant and needs a dry rest through the warmer months, the same rhythm as other spring-ephemeral fawn lilies.

directions: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in well-drained, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; allow the site to dry out somewhat once the foliage yellows in early summer. Katakuri is the Japanese counterpart to the North American trout lilies, native to mountain and lowland forests across Japan, where it carpets the forest floor in early spring with nodding, deep pink to lilac-purple, sharply reflexed flowers above mottled purple-brown-and-green leaves. Its corms were historically the traditional source of katakuriko starch used in Japanese cooking, though the wild plant grows so slowly (corms take seven or more years to reach a usable size) that virtually all katakuriko sold today is made from potato starch instead. Plant in generous drifts under deciduous trees for the best spring display; like its American relatives, it resents disturbance once established and is slow to increase.

planting.note: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, humus-rich soil in full sun to partial shade; Semiplena is a heirloom double-flowered sport of great camas grown since the 19th century and holds its creamy-yellow blooms longer than the single-flowered species.

directions: Plant bulbs 3-4 inches deep in fall in moist, organically rich soil in full sun to partial shade for a late-spring display. Semiplena is a long-cultivated double-flowered form of great camas in which each star-shaped bloom carries extra creamy-yellow to ivory tepals, giving the flower spike a fuller, longer-lasting appearance than the single-flowered species since the doubled, largely sterile flowers do not quickly fade and set seed. Because it rarely sets viable seed, Semiplena is propagated only by division of the bulb's offsets, so plants sold under this name are always genetically identical to the original heirloom clone. Grow it exactly as you would the species, in moist spring soil that can dry out somewhat by midsummer, in a naturalized meadow, wet woodland edge, or mixed border.
